title: Database Indexes: Finding Data Without Scanning Everything

sections.heading: Everyday analogy: the library catalog
sections.body:
Imagine a library with no catalog. To find one book, you check every shelf. That's a full scan - slow.

An index is like a separate, sorted catalog card system. It stores a shortcut: key -> location. A query (a question you ask the database) uses the catalog to jump straight to the right shelf.

- B-Tree / B+ Tree = catalog sorted by title for range searches like "A to M"
- Hash Index = exact match drawer, perfect for "where is book ID 123?"
- Inverted Index = word -> list of books containing that word, for search

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body:
Databases keep data on disk. Reading disk is slow, so we avoid scanning all rows.

An index exists to trade a little extra storage and write work for much faster reads.

Different questions need different catalogs:
- Need range queries? B+ Tree keeps leaves linked and sorted. Used in MySQL, PostgreSQL.
- Need fast writes? LSM Tree (used in Cassandra, RocksDB) writes sequentially, then merges later.
- Need location search? R-Tree handles multi-dimensional spatial data.

sections.heading: What can go wrong
sections.body:
A term: cardinality means how many unique values a column has. Low cardinality = few values like "gender" or "status".

Indexes can hurt if misused:
- Wrong index slows everything: every write must update all indexes.
- Bitmap Index is great for low-cardinality filtering in analytics, but terrible for high-cardinality or heavy writes.
- Hash Index cannot do range queries, only equality.

Too many indexes = slow writes, large storage, and the database picks the wrong catalog.

steps.narration: A query asks for specific data, not the whole table.
We pick an index type that matches the question: range, exact, text, or spatial.
The index is a small, sorted shortcut from key to location.
We jump directly to the data on disk, avoiding a full scan.
On every write, we must also update the index, which costs time and space.

quiz.q: Which index is best for finding all orders with price between $10 and $50?
quiz.why: B+ Tree keeps data sorted with linked leaves, so range scans are fast. Hash Index only does equality.

quiz.q: What fails first if writes grow 100x and you have 10 indexes on the table?
options: Writes slow down sharply as each index must be updated
Inverted Index starts doing range queries
quiz.why: Every write pays a cost to update every index. Too many indexes make high-write workloads very slow and storage-heavy.

quiz.q: Why would you use an Inverted Index?
options: For full-text search: word to documents
quiz.why: Inverted Index maps each keyword to the list of documents containing it, powering Elasticsearch and search engines.
